SOURCE: "ELI5: Long Form Question Answering", Angela Fan, Yacine Jernite, Ethan Perez, David Grangier, Jason Weston, Michael Auli. ACL 2019 (Proceedings pp. 3558–3567), arXiv 1907.09190.

COVERAGE: 39,545 of 39,545 chars read, all 10 pages (pp. 1–9 body, 9–10 references). This PDF is the main paper only. Appendices A (multi-task details), E (rater stability) and F (examples) are referenced but not included. Figures 4, 5, 7 and 8 are images, so their bar values can't be read. I quote only numbers that appear in the running text. Table 3 came out with merged columns, so I split them by position (see PROBLEMS).

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: People preferred the human reference answer over every model in at least 85.5% of pairwise comparisons.
  number: 86% (abstract); at least 85.5% (body)
  setup: crowdworkers saw a question and two answers and judged readability and accuracy. 1000 evaluations, 3 raters each, questions at least 5 words. Two-tailed binomial test, all judgments significant at p=0.05.
  quote: "raters prefer gold re-sponses in over 86% of cases" (p1); "The reference answer is preferred over the output of all of our trained models in at least 85.5% of cases" (p7)
  where: p1 abstract, p7 §6.1
- claim: How the support document is built. The authors pull the top 100 Common Crawl pages per question (Reddit excluded) from a Lucene index, which totals a few hundred thousand words. They then keep the sentences with the highest TF-IDF similarity to the question, add one sentence of context on each side, take 15 passages and concatenate them into a single document.
  number: 100 web sources; 15 passages; ±1 sentence of context
  setup: July 2018 Common Crawl, English only (FastText language ID), Spacy tokenisation, Apache Lucene index.
  quote: "gather the 100 most relevant web sources for each question, excluding Reddit" ... "We find that extracting 15 passages with a context of one sentence before and after the initial selection provides the best trade-off between support document length and likelihood of containing relevant information"
  where: p3 §3.1
- claim: Support documents average 858 words. Answers average 6.6 sentences (130 words), and questions average 42.2 words.
  number: 858 words / 22–60 sentences; 130 words / 6.6 sentences
  setup: whole dataset (Table 1 gives Document 857.6, Answer 130.6, Question 42.2).
  quote: "Support documents contain 22-60 sentences or on average 858 words ... ELI5 contains long-form answers with an average length of 6.6 sentences, or 130 words."
  where: p4 §3.2
- claim: The TF-IDF support document contains the answer only 65% of the time, although 92% contain relevant information. Gold answers fully address the question 94.5% of the time.
  number: 65.0 / 92.0 / 94.5
  setup: 500 random training pairs, annotated by the authors (Table 2).
  quote: "65% of the support docu-ments we construct provide the answer to the ques-tion, and 92% of support documents provide infor-mation relevant to the question."
  where: p4
- claim: Retrieval caps performance. An extractive oracle on the support document reaches 27.4 ROUGE-1, while the same oracle on all 100 web sources reaches 54.8. Fewer than 9% of oracle sentences come from the top-20 TF-IDF passages, so a model would need inputs tens of thousands of words long.
  number: 27.4 vs 54.8 ROUGE-1; <9%
  setup: beam-search oracle choosing up to 10 sentences (beam 10), re-ranked by ROUGE. The rank analysis re-ran selection on 1000 examples with 500 passages.
  quote: "the oracle provides an approximate upper bound of 27.4 ROUGE-1 ... an oracle computed on the full web sources achieves 54.8." (p6); "less than 9% come from the first 20, and most oracles have at least one sentence from the last 100. For a model to perform best, it would have to handle inputs tens of thousands of words long." (p8)
  where: p6 §6.1, p8
- claim: Table 3 test ROUGE-1/2/L, split by column position: Support Document 16.8/2.3/10.2. Nearest Neighbor 16.7/2.3/12.5. Extractive TFIDF 20.6/2.9/17.0. BidAF 23.5/3.1/17.5. LM Q+A 27.8/4.7/23.1 (PPL 42.2). LM Q+D+A 26.4/4.0/20.5 (PPL 33.9). Seq2Seq Q→A 28.3/5.1/22.7 (PPL 52.9). Seq2Seq Q+D→A 28.3/5.1/22.8 (PPL 55.1). Multi-task 28.9/5.4/23.1 (PPL 32.7). Abstractive models score higher on ROUGE, and the Seq2Seq variants barely differ from each other.
  number: see above
  setup: Transformer "big" architecture in fairseq-py, BPE with 40K codes, beam 5, repeated trigrams blocked, min/max length tuned on the validation set.
  quote: "The BidAF model is the strongest ( 23.5)" and "the various Seq2Seq settings do not show large ROUGE differences" (p6). Raw row: "Seq2Seq Multi-task 32.72 8 .95 .42 3 .1"
  where: p6 Table 3, §6.1
- claim: When accuracy was checked against the support document, only 19% of multi-task answers were fully accurate, against 40% of extractive answers. The multi-task answers were more relevant, 84% against 68%.
  number: 19% / 40%; 84% / 68%
  setup: the authors themselves rated 100 answers. Crowdworkers in the accuracy study had no support document.
  quote: "we find 40% of extractive answers to be accurate. We find only 19% of multi-task model answers are fully accurate; even if the model output answers the question, it can generate a sentence with an incorrect statement ... (84% relevancy compared to 68% for extractive)"
  where: p7
- claim: Multi-task Seq2Seq and extractive answers are close in human preference (multi-task preferred 57% of the time). The language model loses to every other system at least 91% of the time.
  quote: "multi-task is only preferred in 57% of comparisons ... the language model, considered worse than any other setting in at least 91% of cases."
  where: p7
- claim: The paper's view of metrics. Perplexity and FILL-1 are poor indicators of full-task quality. Full-answer ROUGE ranks models of similar architecture but "cannot rate an abstractive system against an extractive one". ROUGE-20% (completing the last 20% of an answer) correlates with human judgment. Multi-task scores 37.2 ROUGE-1 on ROUGE-20%, against 26.5 for the LM Q+A.
  quote: "Full answer ROUGE discriminates reasonably well between models with the same general architecture, but cannot rate an abstractive system against an extractive one." (p8); "The lat-ter achieves strong performance of 37.2 ROUGE-1." (p7)
  where: p7–8
- claim: The abstractive model holds up better than the extractive one when the support document overlaps less with the answer (Fig. 7 left, no numbers in the text).
  quote: "the abstrac-tive setting is much better at compensating for when the support document has lower relevance."
  where: p8
- claim: The dedup and split method, which Krishna et al. 2021 later attacked. Validation and test questions were sampled from questions with no close TF-IDF neighbour. Splits are 237K train, 10K valid and 25K test, from 272K questions kept because the question and at least one answer each scored 2 or more upvotes. 63% of questions have other valid answers.
  quote: "sample the validation and test set from the subset which has no close neighbor by TFIDF score. The final dataset contains 237K train examples, 10K for valid, and 25K for test."
  where: p4
- claim: Multi-task training combines LM on Q+D+A, several source/target variants, and masked-word prediction with 15% masking. A task marker is prepended to each sequence.
  quote: "We add a masked word prediction task (Devlin et al. , 2018) where 15% of tokens in the input are masked"
  where: p6 §5.2

LIMITS
- The paper says the best model is "far from human performance", partly because it can't use the full web text, and that the support-document selection "severely limits access to relevant information" (p8).
- The paper concedes ROUGE can't compare extractive and abstractive systems. It never tests whether ROUGE tracks human preference on full answers.
- The 2019 models are pre-trained-free Transformers. No pretrained LM or BART is used, so the scores are dated.
- Only one reference answer per question is used, even though more than half have several.
- TF-IDF dedup is presented as preventing memorisation. Krishna et al. 2021 later showed it fails, but this paper offers no evidence either way.
- Accuracy with the support document visible covers only 100 author-rated examples. No inter-rater agreement is reported for the accuracy or preference studies, only for fluency (in the appendix, not included).
- Faithfulness or citation to the support document is never measured.

BUILDS ON: BidAF (Seo et al., 2017), the Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017), masked-word prediction from BERT (Devlin et al., 2018), ROUGE (Lin, 2004), query-biased multi-document summarisation (Tombros and Sanderson, 1998), WikiSum (Liu et al., 2018), FastText (Bojanowski et al., 2017), FAISS NN search (Johnson et al., 2017), BPE (Sennrich et al., 2016), trigram blocking (Paulus et al., 2017; Fan et al., 2018), large-batch training (Ott et al., 2018), and fairseq (Gehring et al., 2017).

CODE: none in the paper. It points to a support-document script at https://github.com/facebookresearch/ELI5 (p1 footnote).

FIGURES
- Best candidate: Figure 8, p8, "(left) TFIDF rank of source passage for oracle sentences. (right) Highest rank used per question." It shows in one view that useful evidence sits deep in the ranking, which supports the claim that retrieval caps the reader.
- Alternative: Figure 1, p1, "ELI5 example. Models must write multi-sentence answers given questions and supporting web documents." It shows the task shape: a 60-word question, a 327-word answer and a 1070-word support document.

FIT TO NOTES
- 06-generation-for-rag.md fits best. The paper doesn't belong under "Order and size of the context" (around line 202). It belongs next to the FiD paragraph at line 220 as the long-form counterpart. That paragraph says FiD's result holds "on short factoid answers". ELI5 supplies the long-form case: 15 TF-IDF passages (about 858 words), a 27.4 vs 54.8 oracle gap, and fewer than 9% of oracle sentences in the top 20. A second option is "Hallucinations and citations" (line 300), using the 19% fully accurate abstractive vs 40% extractive result and the 84% vs 68% relevance result. Note 06 already mentions ELI5 only through ALCE (Gao et al. 2023). This paper is consistent with ALCE but doesn't repeat it, so citing it here sharpens the note.
- 12-failure-modes.md, "Contamination" (line 201): this paper is the primary source for "ELI5's authors removed near-duplicate questions ... using TF-IDF similarity". It confirms the method (p4), so add it as the citation for that clause. "Measuring the wrong thing" (line 228): the paper partly anticipates Krishna et al. 2021 by conceding that full ROUGE can't compare extractive and abstractive systems. Its own Table 3 also shows nearest-neighbour retrieval at 12.5 ROUGE-L, not far from the extractive models. Nothing in either note contradicts the paper. One tension worth keeping in mind: the paper calls corpus-level ROUGE "useful to rank different related models" (p4), while Krishna shows ROUGE-L can't separate trivial outputs from good ones.

PROBLEMS
- Table 3's columns merged during extraction (for example "32.72 8 .95 .42 3 .1"). I split them by position into PPL / R1 / R2 / RL, and the split agrees with the values quoted in the text (23.5, 27.4, 54.8). Verify against the PDF before quoting R2 or RL values.
- There's an internal inconsistency. §3.1 says 15 passages, but p8 says "extract 500 passages instead of 20".
- Values in Figures 4, 5 and 7 aren't in the text, so the per-system preference matrix and fluency scores aren't available.
- Appendices aren't in this PDF.
- pypdf printed harmless warnings ("Ignoring invalid /FirstChar"). The PDF contains no embedded instructions.
